memos.title: Restore wage–productivity parity.
memos.finding: Since 1973, U.S. productivity has risen 80%. Median worker compensation has risen 14% in real terms. The gap accumulates to roughly $50 trillion in transferred income from labor to capital over five decades.
memos.mechanism: Wages and productivity moved together from 1948 to 1973 because three institutions, sectoral unions, a high minimum wage, and progressive tax brackets, required them to. Each was weakened in the dismantling period documented in the Architecture chapter. Wages now respond to bargaining power, not productivity.
memos.proposal: A federal minimum wage indexed to productivity growth, set at $17/hour and rising with output per hour. Sectoral bargaining rights in care, retail, logistics, and food service, modeled on the European works-council framework. Restoration of the National Labor Relations Board's pre-1978 enforcement budget.
memos.impact: Closes approximately 60% of the wage–productivity gap within a decade per Economic Policy Institute modeling. Raises median real wages by an estimated $14,000/year for non-college workers.
memos.references: Figure 5 (Wages vs. Productivity); Figure 8 ($100 of New Wealth)

memos.title: Tax assets and labor at the same rate.
memos.finding: Capital gains and qualified dividends are taxed at a federal top rate of 20%. Wages at the top rate of 37%. Capital income is concentrated in the top 1% of households, which holds 54% of equities.
memos.mechanism: The differential rate is a 50-year accumulation of carve-outs, the 1978 capital gains cut, the 2003 dividend cut, the 2017 TCJA pass-through deduction, each compounding the others. Asset holders are taxed at less than half the rate of workers earning the same total income.
memos.proposal: Equalize capital and labor tax rates. Implement a mark-to-market regime on unrealized capital gains above $50M, taxed annually at the long-term rate. Restore the estate tax exemption to its 2000 level ($1M, indexed to inflation).
memos.impact: Raises an estimated $3.9 trillion over ten years per CBO scoring of similar proposals. Reverses the post-1980 concentration of wealth at the top decile by an estimated 4–6 percentage points.
memos.references: Figure 8 ($100 of New Wealth); the Architecture timeline

memos.title: Match the GI Bill, for the populations it excluded.
memos.finding: The 1944 GI Bill transferred roughly $400 billion (in 2024 dollars) of asset support to predominantly white veterans between 1944 and 1956. The Black–white wealth ratio has moved from 9¢ to 12¢ in the 35 years since systematic measurement began.
memos.mechanism: Wealth compounds from a starting balance. The descendants of GI Bill recipients inherited assets that compounded across two generations. The descendants of those excluded compounded nothing. The wealth gap is not an income problem; it is a compounding problem.
memos.proposal: A federal asset-matching program for Black households, paid at age 18, structured as a baby bond capped at $40,000, financed by the equalized capital gains rate proposed in Memo II. Indexed to the wealth gap closure rate so the program adjusts as the gap closes.
memos.impact: Closes approximately 30% of the Black–white median wealth gap within one generation. Estimated cost: $80B/year over 18 years.
memos.references: Figure 13 (The Asset Gap, sticky scroll); Memo II

memos.title: Build a public option in housing.
memos.finding: Housing costs have risen 4.2× since 1960 in real terms while household income has risen 1.6×. Homeownership rates have not meaningfully changed in 60 years. In the Bay Area, NYC, Boston, and Seattle, even median-plus incomes cannot afford median housing.
memos.mechanism: Housing is treated as both a place to live and a primary asset. These uses are in direct conflict, appreciation requires scarcity, but shelter requires abundance. The U.S. has resolved this conflict in favor of asset appreciation since the 1980s.
memos.proposal: A federal public housing authority chartered to build 1.5 million units over a decade, financed at Treasury rates, structured as permanent affordability (Vienna model) rather than market-rate units with subsidy. Co-op ownership pathways. Direct federal land use override of local zoning above a population threshold.
memos.impact: Reduces housing cost burden below 30% of income for an estimated 18 million households. Brings U.S. social housing share from 0.7% to 5% of total stock, still below France (17%), Singapore (78%), or Vienna (43%).

memos.title: Decommodify the work of raising the next generation.
memos.finding: Surveyed Americans say they want 2.7 children. They have 1.6. They cite cost as the primary reason. Childcare costs more than rent in most U.S. cities. The U.S. is the only OECD country without federal paid parental leave.
memos.mechanism: Care work was historically performed by women inside households, uncompensated and invisible to the economy. As women entered the formal labor market, care was monetized but never socialized. The result is a system where families pay full private cost for a service that produces an unambiguously public good.
memos.proposal: Universal pre-K from age 3. A federal childcare benefit capping family cost at 7% of household income. Twelve weeks federally funded parental leave at 80% of prior wages. Long-term care benefit for elder care.
memos.impact: Closes the fertility gap by an estimated 400,000 births/year. Raises female labor force participation by 4 percentage points (CBO). Federal cost: approximately $80 billion/year, partially offset by increased tax revenue from the larger workforce.
memos.references: Figure 10 (Way of Life, multigenerational households, fertility)

memos.title: Decouple healthcare from employment.
memos.finding: U.S. healthcare costs rose 8.4× in real terms since 1960, the steepest of any basket component. Medical debt is the leading cause of personal bankruptcy. Employer-tied insurance creates the largest structural friction in U.S. labor mobility.
memos.mechanism: Healthcare was tied to employment by accident during WWII wage controls, then made permanent by the 1954 tax exclusion of employer health benefits. The arrangement converts a public-good service into an employer perk and converts workers into hostages of their current job.
memos.proposal: A public option open to any U.S. resident, priced at Medicare rates plus 10%. Voluntary enrollment, no employer-tied requirement. Pharmaceutical negotiation extended from Medicare to the full public option. Cost transparency requirements for all hospital-billed services.
memos.impact: Reduces national health spending by an estimated 12–18% per CBO scoring of similar proposals. Increases voluntary job mobility by an estimated 22% (NBER). Coverage approaches universal within five years.

memos.title: Keep capital local, where it was extracted.
memos.finding: The five mechanism geographies, racial exclusion, extractive abandonment, manufacturing collapse, colonial baseline, and asset-economy edges, each experienced systematic capital outflow. The Mississippi Delta, McDowell County, Mahoning County, and Pine Ridge all share the same pattern: a period of extraction followed by abandonment.
memos.mechanism: American capital is mobile. Local labor is not. When an investment thesis stops paying, coal exhausted, manufacturing offshored, agriculture mechanized, capital leaves. The community does not. The infrastructure stays. The houses stay. The people stay. Only the economy that made them all viable departs.
memos.proposal: Federal seeding of community development financial institutions (CDFIs) in geographies identified by the Five Americas typology. Capital must remain in the originating community. Returns reinvest locally. Model: the Bank of North Dakota (public state bank, 1919–present), Mondragon (worker-owned industrial federation), Vienna's municipal housing trust.
memos.impact: Estimated 200,000 jobs created in target communities over a decade. Reverses out-migration in the five mechanism geographies. Cost: $25B in federal seed capital, recycled within affected economies.
memos.references: Figures 1, 4, 4B (Five Americas atlas + Mahoning County pictogram)
